kurals.tamil:
அன்புடைமை ஆன்ற குடிப்பிறத்தல் வேந்தவாம்
பண்புடைமை தூதுரைப்பான் பண்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Anbudaimai aandra kudippiraththal vendhavaam
Panbudaimai thoodhuraippaan panbu.
kurals.meaning: An envoy should have three things: a loving nature, birth in a family of good standing, and the kind of refined conduct that kings value.
kurals.elementary: When your class sends someone to ask the principal for a longer break, you pick a kind person who comes from a family everyone trusts and who knows how to be polite to grown-ups. The person carrying a message has to be someone the listener already respects.
kurals.university: The chapter on the envoy (tūtu) belongs to the Amaichiyal, the section on ministers (chs. 64-73), and opens with the general qualifications. Parimelazhagar glosses aṉpuṭaimai as affection toward one’s own kin (cuṟṟattār), ‘āṉṟa kuṭi’ as a family fit to bear ministerial office, and ‘vēntu avām paṇpu’ as the qualities royalty desires. He adds that kin-affection means the envoy keeps his relatives from harm, and good lineage means he has heard of envoy-craft from his forebears. Manakkudavar reads the first quality differently, as love for one’s own king, and explains ‘qualities kings desire’ as not coveting what the king covets. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar keep the three-part list, Pappaiah widening the love to people, state and kin. On the text: ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print அன்புடைமை ஆன்ற; the sandhi-joined text at thirukkural-thamizh.org reads அன்புடைமை யான்ற, the same words with the glide written in.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him also appoint an ambassador who is versed in all sciences, who understands hints, expressions of the face and gestures, who is honest, skilful, and of (noble) family.”
hinduism.explanation: The Laws of Manu tell the king how to choose his envoy, and good family is on the list along with learning, honesty and skill.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Manu makes noble birth one of the envoy’s basic qualifications.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 7.63 (trans. G. Bühler, Sacred Books of the East vol. 25)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Direct match on noble family and on character, but Manu does not name affection for kin.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore, brethren, look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business.”
christianity.explanation: When the apostles need people to act on the community’s behalf, they ask for men already known for good reputation and wisdom.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, a person is sent to represent others because of character that people already recognize.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the idea of choosing representatives for proven character, but the task is administrative, not a diplomatic mission.

islam.quote_or_event: “I asked you about his family and your reply was that he belonged to a very noble family. In fact all the Apostles come from noble families amongst their respective peoples.”
islam.explanation: Questioning Abu Sufyan about the Prophet, the Byzantine emperor Heraclius treats noble lineage as a mark of a genuine messenger.
islam.tie_back: Heraclius and the Kural both assume that a trustworthy messenger comes from a respected family.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on lineage as the credential of a messenger, though the subject is a prophet rather than a royal envoy.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that loveth pureness of heart, for the grace of his lips the king shall be his friend.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb says a person with a pure heart and gracious speech wins the friendship of kings.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s ‘quality that kings love’ (vēntu avām paṇpu): good character and pleasant manners.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close fit to the third quality; says nothing about lineage or envoys as such.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Among the highest blessings the Buddha lists in the Mangala Sutta are supporting one’s parents, cherishing spouse and children, and helping one’s relatives.
buddhism.explanation: The discourse treats care for one’s own kin as a mark of a well-ordered and admirable life.
buddhism.tie_back: It matches Parimelazhagar’s reading of aṉpuṭaimai as affection for one’s own kin.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Matches only the kin-affection element and does not concern envoys.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When the Greeks send an embassy to the angry Achilles, Nestor has Phoenix lead it. Phoenix is the old man who raised Achilles, and he later appeals to that bond of love.
greek_mythology.explanation: Phoenix is chosen for his loving relationship with Achilles, which the Greeks hope will make the hearer receptive.
greek_mythology.tie_back: In the Kural too, affection and good standing are what qualify someone to carry a message.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Real envoy episode showing affection as a qualification, but here the affection is toward the hearer, not the envoy’s own kin.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In his essay ‘Of Negotiating’, Francis Bacon advises using agents who have a personal attachment to the business they are sent on, and matching the agent’s temperament to the task.
philosophy.explanation: Bacon argues that a negotiator who cares about the cause works harder at it, and that personal qualities should be chosen to fit the mission.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Bacon judges an envoy first by character and attachment, and only then by skill.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory of Bacon’s essay; the general idea fits, but lineage and royal manners are absent.

kurals.tamil:
அன்பறிவு ஆராய்ந்த சொல்வன்மை தூதுரைப்பார்க்கு
இன்றி யமையாத மூன்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Anbarivu aaraaindha solvanmai thoodhuraippaarkku
Indri yamaiyaadha moondru.
kurals.meaning: Love for one’s king, knowledge of what serves him, and skill in choosing the right words are the three things an envoy cannot do without.
kurals.elementary: Imagine you are sent to ask the neighbours to give back your family’s ball. You need three things. You have to care about your family, you have to know exactly what to ask for, and you have to pick your words well so the neighbours say yes.
kurals.university: The couplet names three indispensable (iṉṟiyamaiyāta) qualities. Parimelazhagar makes each one specific: aṉpu is love for one’s own king, aṟivu is knowing what is good for him, and ārāynta colvaṉmai is careful speech before foreign kings. He explains the ‘examining’ (ārāytal) as choosing words the other side will agree to. From ‘indispensable three’ he infers that the ministerial virtues listed earlier are also needed. He also notes that 681 and 682 give the general marks common to both kinds of envoy the chapter goes on to separate. Solomon Pappaiah reads aṉpu as love of country, and Kalaignar gives a plain list. The couplet looks back to chapter 65 (Colvaṉmai, power of speech). On the text: the sandhi-joined text at thirukkural-thamizh.org runs the words together (அன்பறி வாராய்ந்த … தூதுரைப்பார்க் கின்றி யமையாத), with no change of wording.

hinduism.quote_or_event: On first meeting Hanuman, Rama tells Lakshmana that someone who speaks like this must have mastered the Vedas and grammar, because in a long speech he made not one error, and his words would win over even an enemy with a raised sword.
hinduism.explanation: Hanuman comes to Rama as Sugriva’s envoy. His devotion, knowledge and flawless, well-chosen speech make Rama trust him at once.
hinduism.tie_back: Hanuman has all three of the Kural’s essentials: love for his master, knowledge, and carefully chosen speech.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close thematic match to a real envoy scene; wording is a paraphrase.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Now then we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us: we pray you in Christ’s stead, be ye reconciled to God.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes apostles as ambassadors who speak on another’s behalf and plead with their hearers to be reconciled.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s envoy, the ambassador is moved by love for the one who sends him (2 Cor 5:14) and has to speak persuasively.
christianity._accuracy_note: Explicit ambassador language and a persuasive task; the three qualities are implied rather than listed.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Moses] said, ‘My Lord, expand for me my breast [with assurance] And ease for me my task And untie the knot from my tongue That they may understand my speech.’”
islam.explanation: Before going to Pharaoh as God’s envoy, Moses asks for confidence and clear, understandable speech.
islam.tie_back: Moses treats power of speech as indispensable to the mission, just as the Kural does.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on speech as essential to an envoy; love and knowledge are not addressed in the verses.

judaism.quote_or_event: Sent to Pharaoh, Moses protests that he is ‘slow of speech’. God appoints his brother Aaron to be his spokesman, so the message is delivered with both Moses’ knowledge and Aaron’s eloquence.
judaism.explanation: The Torah treats the mission to Pharaoh as needing a good speaker, and supplies one when the envoy himself lacks the skill.
judaism.tie_back: It shows the Kural’s claim that speaking skill is indispensable, not optional, for an envoy.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good match on eloquence as a requirement; the Kural’s pairing with love and knowledge is only implicit.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “It’s a mendicant who learns and educates others. They memorize and remember. They understand and help others understand.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists the qualities that make a monk fit to go on a mission, and names Sāriputta as having them.
buddhism.tie_back: Learning, understanding and the ability to make others understand match the Kural’s knowledge and discerning speech.
buddhism.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.16, Dūteyya Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)
buddhism._accuracy_note: An explicit list of envoy qualifications; ‘love’ appears only indirectly as ‘they don’t cause quarrels’.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Trojan elder Antenor recalls how Odysseus came to Troy as an envoy: he stood with his eyes fixed on the ground, but when he spoke, his words fell like winter snowflakes and no mortal could rival him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer presents Odysseus as the model of an envoy’s eloquence.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the Kural’s ārāynta colvaṉmai, carefully weighed speech, at its best.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A real envoy scene focused on eloquence; love and knowledge are not the point.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle says a speaker earns trust through three things: practical wisdom (phronēsis), virtue (aretē), and goodwill toward the audience (eunoia).
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, persuasion depends on the speaker’s character as well as the argument.
philosophy.tie_back: His goodwill, wisdom and skilled speech line up closely with the Kural’s love, knowledge and chosen words.
philosophy._accuracy_note: A striking three-part parallel, though Aristotle’s goodwill is toward the audience, not toward one’s own king.

kurals.tamil:
நூலாருள் நூல்வல்லன் ஆகுதல் வேலாருள்
வென்றி வினையுரைப்பான் பண்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Noolaarul noolvallan aagudhal velaarul
Vendri vinaiyuraippaan panbu.
kurals.meaning: Someone who goes among spear-bearing kings to argue for his own king’s success must be the most accomplished scholar even among the learned.
kurals.elementary: If you have to explain your team’s plan to the biggest, toughest team in the playground, you had better know the rules of the game better than anyone there. Knowing more than the clever people is what keeps you safe in front of the strong ones.
kurals.university: The couplet contrasts two audiences: nūlār, those learned in the treatises, and vēlār, the spear-bearers. Parimelazhagar identifies the first as the foreign court’s ministers, learned in nīti-nūl (works on polity), and the second as foreign kings. He says Valluvar wrote ‘vēlār’ to evoke their readiness to kill (kōṟal mālaiyar), and ‘veṉṟi viṉai’ to cover both kinds of envoy’s work. To be ‘vallaṉ’ (master) is more than knowing the texts: it is being able to set them out and apply them in front of ministers who only know them. Manakkudavar reads nūlāruḷ nūlvallaṉ as being able to expound all the texts before the learned. Pappaiah stresses knowledge of political ethics in a hostile court. On the text: the sandhi-joined text reads நூலாரு ணூல்வல்ல னாகுதல், the same words as the split form (நூலாருள் நூல்வல்லன் ஆகுதல்) in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Before the war, Krishna goes as the Pandavas’ envoy to the Kaurava court. In front of Bhishma, Drona, Vidura and the assembled warriors, he argues for peace from dharma and statecraft. Duryodhana plots to seize him.
hinduism.explanation: The most learned of counsellors speaks in a hall full of armed kings, pressing his side’s case while in danger himself.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s picture: learning greater than the learned, used among spear-bearers for one’s own side’s success.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Bhagavat-yana sections (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: The classic Indian embassy and a very close match; summarised, not quoted.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And as he thus spake for himself, Festus said with a loud voice, Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad.”
christianity.explanation: Paul, calling himself an ambassador, defends his message before the Roman governor Festus and King Agrippa, and his learning is so plain that Festus remarks on it.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s envoy, Paul stands before men of armed power and is marked out by superior learning.
christianity._accuracy_note: Real scene of learned speech before rulers; Paul is defending himself, not negotiating for a king.

islam.quote_or_event: When the Quraysh sent envoys to the Negus of Abyssinia to demand the Muslim emigrants, Ja‘far ibn Abi Talib answered for the Muslims before the king and his bishops. He explained their faith and recited from Surat Maryam, and the Negus refused to hand them over.
islam.explanation: Ja‘far’s learned, measured answer in a foreign court won protection for his people against an armed opponent’s embassy.
islam.tie_back: He shows the Kural’s ideal: mastery of one’s own teaching, used among powerful rulers to win the case.
islam.source: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (trans. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad)
islam._accuracy_note: Well-attested sira episode; Ja‘far acts as spokesman for refugees rather than as a king’s envoy.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And in all matters of wisdom and understanding, that the king enquired of them, he found them ten times better than all the magicians and astrologers that were in all his realm.”
judaism.explanation: Daniel and his companions, exiles at a foreign court, prove more learned than all of Babylon’s scholars.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s nūlāruḷ nūlvallaṉ: foremost among the learned, in front of a powerful foreign king.
judaism._accuracy_note: Exact match on excelling among the learned at a foreign court; Daniel is a courtier, not an envoy.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When the Greek king Milinda invites the monk Nāgasena to debate, Nāgasena agrees only if the king will talk as a scholar does, not as a king does. Kings punish those who disagree; scholars can be refuted without anger.
buddhism.explanation: The learned monk faces a powerful king and relies on learning to set fair terms before answering the king’s hard questions.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s envoy, Nāgasena uses learning to hold his ground before a king who could use force.
buddhism.source: Milindapañha, Book II (trans. T. W. Rhys Davids, The Questions of King Milinda)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on learning before armed power; Nāgasena is a debater, not an envoy.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Homeric Hymn to Hermes, the infant Hermes steals Apollo’s cattle. Brought before Zeus, he talks his way out with clever speech and wins Apollo over with the lyre he has invented. He becomes the messenger and herald of the gods.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hermes, the divine herald, is a figure of cleverness and skilled speech who can win over more powerful gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The god of messengers succeeds, as the Kural says an envoy must, by outdoing the clever in wit and learning.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Right archetype (the divine herald), but the hymn is about his cunning, not diplomatic learning.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero has Crassus argue that no one can be a complete orator without knowledge of all the important subjects and arts, because eloquence without substance is empty noise.
philosophy.explanation: For Cicero, persuasive speech in public affairs rests on wide learning.
philosophy.tie_back: It fits the Kural’s demand that the envoy be the most learned among the learned.
philosophy._accuracy_note: A general theory of the learned orator, not specific to envoys; paraphrased.

kurals.tamil:
அறிவுரு வாராய்ந்த கல்விஇம் மூன்றன்
செறிவுடையான் செல்க வினைக்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Arivuru vaaraaindha kalvi-im moondran
Serivudaiyaan selga vinaikku.
kurals.meaning: Let the person who combines three things go on the mission: natural good sense, an impressive appearance, and learning that has been tested.
kurals.elementary: To show the new kid around school, the teacher picks someone who is smart, looks neat and friendly, and has learned the school rules properly. Someone with only one of these would not be enough. You need all three together.
kurals.university: Parimelazhagar makes each of the three precise. Aṟivu is innate intelligence (iyaṟkai aṟivu). Uru is a presence that viewers find attractive (kaṇṭār virumpum tōṟṟap polivu). Ārāynta kalvi is learning that has been examined ‘with many, over a long time’. The key word is ceṟivu, ‘combination’ or ‘density’: he notes that the three rarely come together in one person, and that together they make the envoy respected, so the mission succeeds. ‘Viṉai’ is the business of embassy to foreign kings. Manakkudavar reads ceṟivu as ‘containment’ (aṭakkam). Pappaiah adds that the person should be able to frame his message himself, which anticipates the ‘self-composing’ envoy of 687. On the text: ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print கல்விஇம் மூன்றன் (a vowel hiatus); the sandhi-joined text at thirukkural-thamizh.org reads கல்வியிம் மூன்றன், with the glide y written in.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “(Such) an ambassador is commended to a king (who is) loyal, honest, skilful, possessing a good memory, who knows the (proper) place and time (for action, who is) handsome, fearless, and eloquent.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu lists appearance next to memory, skill and eloquence as qualifications for an envoy.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s aṟivu, uru and kalvi, Manu counts a good appearance as a real qualification alongside intelligence and learning.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 7.64 (trans. G. Bühler, Sacred Books of the East vol. 25)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: an envoy’s appearance, intelligence and skill are named together.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man.”
christianity.explanation: Luke describes the young Jesus growing in wisdom and in bodily stature together, and winning people’s favour.
christianity.tie_back: Wisdom, bearing and the goodwill they earn are the combination the Kural looks for in an envoy.
christianity._accuracy_note: Same combination of wisdom and stature, but not about envoys or missions.

islam.quote_or_event: Dihya al-Kalbi, whom the Prophet sent with his letter to the Byzantine ruler, was known for his striking good looks. Umm Salama mistook the angel Gabriel for Dihya, calling him ‘a handsome person amongst the companions’.
islam.explanation: The early community’s envoy to the emperor was remembered for his fine appearance.
islam.tie_back: The Kural lists uru, an impressive presence, as part of what makes an envoy respected abroad.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 7 (Dihya carries the letter); Sahih al-Bukhari 3634 (his handsome appearance)
islam._accuracy_note: Both facts are attested, but no source says his appearance was why he was chosen.

judaism.quote_or_event: “That is cunning in playing, and a mighty valiant man, and a man of war, and prudent in matters, and a comely person, and the LORD is with him.”
judaism.explanation: Saul’s servant recommends David for royal service by listing skill, courage, good judgement and good looks.
judaism.tie_back: Prudence, comeliness and cultivated skill are a close match for the Kural’s aṟivu, uru and kalvi.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close list of qualities for someone presented to a king, though the post is court musician, not envoy.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Sāriputta was won over to the Dhamma when he saw the monk Assaji on his alms round and was struck by his calm, graceful bearing. He asked him who his teacher was and received a short verse of teaching.
buddhism.explanation: Assaji’s outward bearing opened the way, and his wisdom finished the work.
buddhism.tie_back: Presence first earns respect and learning then carries the message, as the Kural expects of an envoy.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Illustrates bearing plus wisdom winning a hearer; Assaji was not on a formal mission.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Before Odysseus appears before the Phaeacians, Athena makes him taller and sturdier-looking so that he will be welcomed, feared and respected, and will succeed in the contests ahead.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer treats appearance as something that decides how a stranger pleading his cause will be received.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This matches Parimelazhagar’s point that uru helps the envoy be well regarded, and so helps the mission succeed.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Clear case of appearance helping someone who needs a foreign court’s favour; Odysseus is a suppliant, not an envoy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates says the nature fit for the highest training must be quick to learn, have a good memory, and be high-minded and gracious. Such natural gifts, perfected by education and maturity, deserve to be entrusted with the state.
philosophy.explanation: Plato holds that the best public servant joins natural talent with long, tested education.
philosophy.tie_back: This is close to the Kural’s pairing of innate aṟivu with ārāynta kalvi, learning examined over time.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches the pairing of nature and education; appearance and embassy are not discussed.

kurals.tamil:
தொகச்சொல்லித் தூவாத நீக்கி நகச்சொல்லி
நன்றி பயப்பதாந் தூது.
kurals.transliteration:
Thogachchollith thoovaadha neekki nagachcholli
Nandri payappadhaan thoodhu.
kurals.meaning: The true envoy sums many matters up briefly, leaves out harsh words, says things so pleasantly that the listeners smile, and so wins benefit for his master.
kurals.elementary: If you need to tell a friend they broke your toy, you don’t list every bad thing they ever did. You say it short, you leave out the mean words, and you say it kindly, maybe with a smile. Then they are much more likely to help fix it.
kurals.university: Parimelazhagar reads the three verbs as two techniques. Tokac colli is condensing: when many demands must be made, state the one cause from which they all follow, so the other side agrees because the point is short and has to be worked out. Tūvāta nīkki naka colli applies to unwelcome demands: drop the harsh words (veyya col) and put things so pleasantly that the listener agrees without feeling the sting. Both serve naṉṟi payattal, securing benefit for one’s own king. Manakkudavar says the couplet teaches ‘how to speak’. Kalaignar glosses tūvāta as what would provoke anger, and Varadarasanar as what is useless. The couplet repeats the ideals of chapter 65 on speech, applied to diplomacy. On the text: all sources agree; the final தூது follows நன்றி பயப்பதாம் with the m assimilated (பயப்பதாந்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Austerity of speech consists in speaking words that are truthful, pleasing, beneficial, and not agitating to others, and also in regularly reciting Vedic literature.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita defines disciplined speech as true, pleasant, helpful, and free of anything that disturbs the listener.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural gives the envoy the same pattern: leave out words that wound, speak pleasantly, and bring benefit.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.15 (Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close match on pleasing, non-agitating, beneficial speech; not specific to diplomacy.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers to speak graciously and aptly to outsiders so that they can answer each person well.
christianity.tie_back: Gracious, well-seasoned speech to outsiders is the envoy’s craft the Kural describes.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on gracious speech; condensing is not mentioned.

islam.quote_or_event: “Go, both of you, to Pharaoh. Indeed, he has transgressed. And speak to him with gentle speech that perhaps he may be reminded or fear [Allah].”
islam.explanation: God sends Moses and Aaron as envoys to a tyrant and tells them to speak gently so that he might listen.
islam.tie_back: Softening a hard message so that a hostile ruler will listen is exactly the Kural’s tūvāta nīkki.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close: envoys told to deliver an unwelcome message to a king in gentle words.

judaism.quote_or_event: “By long forbearing is a prince persuaded, and a soft tongue breaketh the bone.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb teaches that patience and gentle speech can persuade a ruler and overcome even the hardest resistance.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s envoy likewise wins over a foreign king with soft words.
judaism._accuracy_note: Direct match on persuading a ruler by gentle speech.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha says speech with five qualities is well spoken: it is said at the right time, it is true, it is said gently, it is beneficial, and it is said with a mind of goodwill.
buddhism.explanation: Good speech in the Buddha’s teaching is timely, true, gentle and beneficial.
buddhism.tie_back: Gentle and beneficial speech is the Kural’s naka colli … naṉṟi payattal.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Matches gentleness and benefit; brevity and the diplomatic setting are absent.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Agamemnon’s offer to Achilles ends with a demand that Achilles yield to him as the more kingly man. When Odysseus repeats the offer to Achilles, he lists the gifts but quietly leaves out that insulting demand.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus edits his king’s message and drops the part that would only anger the hearer, so the offer has a better chance.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is tūvāta nīkki, leaving out the harsh words, carried out by Homer’s model envoy.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Almost exact: an envoy removing offensive words from his master’s message for the master’s benefit.

philosophy.quote_or_event: François de Callières, a French diplomat, advised that a good negotiator should put things agreeably, keep his temper, and never offend a prince with harsh words, because a well-turned phrase wins more than a blunt demand.
philosophy.explanation: Callières’ early handbook of diplomacy treats pleasant, tactful speech as a working tool.
philosophy.tie_back: His advice closely matches the Kural’s envoy, who speaks so as to please while pursuing his master’s gain.
philosophy.source: François de Callières, De la manière de négocier avec les souverains (1716)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the treatise’s general advice; wording is not quoted.

kurals.tamil:
கற்றுக்கண் அஞ்சான் செலச்சொல்லிக் காலத்தால்
தக்கது அறிவதாம் தூது.
kurals.transliteration:
Katrukkan anjaan selachchollik kaalaththaal
Thakkadhu arivadhaam thoodhu.
kurals.meaning: The true envoy is well learned, speaks so that his words sink in, does not flinch at angry looks, and knows what the moment calls for.
kurals.elementary: Sometimes when you explain something important, the other person frowns at you. A brave messenger doesn’t run away or start stammering. They keep calm, say it clearly so it is understood, and think about what will work best right then.
kurals.university: Parimelazhagar rearranges the clauses: kaṟṟu (having studied the works on polity), cela colli (speaking so the enemy king takes the message to heart), kaṇ añcāṉ (not fearing his glare, ceyirttu nōkku), and kālattāl takkatu aṟivatu (knowing the means suited to the time). He explains why learning comes first: it teaches the means (upāyam), and if the moment calls for another method, the envoy must be able to change course. Manakkudavar gives kaṟṟu a narrower sense, having learned how to calm a foreign king who becomes angry. Pappaiah calls the timely skill a strategic path (tantira vazhi). ‘Kaṇ añcāṉ’ goes back to the Sangam ideal of the unflinching gaze (vaṉkaṇ), which returns in 689. On the text: ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net read காலத்தால் / தக்கது அறிவதாம்; the sandhi-joined text reads கற்றுக்கண் ணஞ்சான் … காலத்தாற் / றக்க தறிவதாந் தூது, the same wording.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Captured and brought bound before Ravana, Hanuman speaks without fear. He declares himself Rama’s envoy and warns Ravana to return Sita. When Ravana orders his death, Vibhishana objects that an envoy may not be killed.
hinduism.explanation: Hanuman delivers his master’s warning to the face of an enraged king, with learning and nerve.
hinduism.tie_back: He embodies the Kural’s envoy who ‘does not fear the eye’ and makes his words sink in.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near-perfect narrative match: a learned envoy, fearless under a hostile king’s glare.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And for me, that utterance may be given unto me, that I may open my mouth boldly, to make known the mystery of the gospel, For which I am an ambassador in bonds: that therein I may speak boldly, as I ought to speak.”
christianity.explanation: In prison, Paul calls himself an ‘ambassador in bonds’ and asks for boldness to speak his message as he should.
christianity.tie_back: Paul’s bold speech under hostile power is the Kural’s kaṇ añcāṉ, the envoy who does not quail.
christianity._accuracy_note: Explicit ambassador language with fearless speech; the timely-strategy element is absent.

islam.quote_or_event: Before the battle of al-Qadisiyya, the Muslim envoy Rib‘i ibn ‘Amir rode into the Persian commander Rustam’s richly carpeted tent. Unimpressed by its splendour, he calmly stated his side’s terms and aims.
islam.explanation: Early histories remember Rib‘i as unafraid of the display and power of the Persian court.
islam.tie_back: He fits the Kural’s envoy who is not cowed by a hostile ruler’s gaze and delivers his message whole.
islam.source: al-Tabari, Tarikh al-rusul wa-l-muluk (History of al-Tabari, vol. 12: The Battle of al-Qadisiyyah)
islam._accuracy_note: Famous envoy episode in al-Tabari; the details come through later historical tradition.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Pharaoh said unto him, Get thee from me, take heed to thyself, see my face no more; for in that day thou seest my face thou shalt die. And Moses said, Thou hast spoken well, I will see thy face again no more.”
judaism.explanation: Threatened with death if he appears again, Moses answers Pharaoh calmly and without fear.
judaism.tie_back: Moses does not fear the king’s angry face, which is the Kural’s kaṇ añcāṉ almost word for word.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match on fearlessness before a hostile king’s face.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “They don’t tremble when arriving at an assembly of fierce debaters. … and they don’t tremble when questioned.”
buddhism.explanation: In the verses on the qualified envoy, the Buddha says such a monk is not shaken by a hostile assembly or by hard questions.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Buddhist form of the Kural’s kaṇ añcāṉ: steadiness in front of hostile listeners.
buddhism.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.16, Dūteyya Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Explicit envoy text on fearlessness before a fierce audience.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Priam goes alone to the tent of Achilles, the man who killed his son. He faces Achilles’ temper, kisses his hands, and, choosing his moment and his words, persuades him to give back Hector’s body.
greek_mythology.explanation: Priam, acting as his own envoy, faces a dangerous and angry enemy and wins his request through courage and well-judged speech.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He shows the Kural’s trio: no fear of the fierce gaze, words that sink in, and a sense of what the moment needs.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong match in courage and timing; Priam pleads for himself rather than for a sovereign.

philosophy.quote_or_event: At his trial, Socrates refuses to flatter or plead before an angry Athenian jury. He says he would rather die than speak in a way unworthy of himself.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates speaks the truth plainly to a hostile audience and ignores the threat to his life.
philosophy.tie_back: Fearlessness before angry listeners is the Kural’s kaṇ añcāṉ.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Right virtue, but Socrates speaks in his own defence, not as an envoy.

kurals.tamil:
கடனறிந்து காலங் கருதி இடனறிந்து
எண்ணி உரைப்பான் தலை.
kurals.transliteration:
Kadanarindhu kaalang karudhi idanarindhu
Enni uraippaan thalai.
kurals.meaning: The best envoy knows the proper protocol, waits for the right moment, picks the right place, and thinks his words through before he speaks.
kurals.elementary: If you want to ask your parents for a puppy, the smartest way is to wait until they are relaxed, not in the middle of a busy morning. Pick a good spot, and practise what you will say and what they might answer. That is how the best messengers do it.
kurals.university: Parimelazhagar glosses kaṭaṉ as the proper conduct toward foreign kings, which comes from weighing their standing, one’s own king’s and one’s own. Kālam is their cevvi, the mood in which they are receptive. Iṭaṉ is a place where one’s supporters are at hand. Eṇṇi means rehearsing in advance one’s own words, the other side’s likely replies, and one’s counter-replies. He says Valluvar chose ‘talai’ (the foremost) because the Sanskrit treatises (vaṭanūlār) rank envoys as first, middle and last, the last being a mere letter-carrier. With this couplet ends the section (681-687) on the envoy who frames his own words (tāṉ vakuttuk kūṟuvāṉ). The following three couplets deal with the envoy who repeats a given message. Manakkudavar likewise calls this the mark of the foremost envoy. On the text: the sandhi-joined text reads கருதி யிடனறிந் / தெண்ணி யுரைப்பான் றலை, the same wording.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya ranks envoys in three grades: one with full ministerial qualifications who may negotiate on his own judgement (nisṛṣṭārtha), one lacking a quarter of those qualities who is limited to a set commission (parimitārtha), and one lacking half who only carries messages (śāsanahara).
hinduism.explanation: The Arthashastra grades envoys by how much they may frame the message themselves.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Sanskrit three-grade scheme (talai, iṭai, kaṭai) that Parimelazhagar says Valluvar alludes to with ‘talai’.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Direct source for the classification the commentator cites; summarised rather than quoted.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.”
christianity.explanation: Sending out his disciples, Jesus tells them to combine shrewd judgement with innocence among hostile hearers.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s foremost envoy is also shrewd about time and place while doing no harm.
christianity._accuracy_note: Captures the prudence of those sent out; time, place and rehearsal are not spelled out.

islam.quote_or_event: “Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction, and argue with them in a way that is best.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an tells the Prophet to deliver his message with wisdom and to argue in the most fitting manner.
islam.tie_back: ‘Wisdom’ and ‘the way that is best’ correspond to the Kural’s careful weighing of duty, moment and manner.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches considered, well-judged delivery; the specific mention of time and place is missing.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And there was set meat before him to eat: but he said, I will not eat, until I have told mine errand. And he said, Speak on.”
judaism.explanation: Abraham’s servant, sent to find a wife for Isaac, will not eat until he has delivered his mission. He then tells it in a carefully arranged way.
judaism.tie_back: He knows his duty (kaṭaṉ aṟintu) and chooses his moment and words, like the Kural’s foremost envoy.
judaism._accuracy_note: A genuine envoy scene showing duty and deliberate speech.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When Devadatta split the Sangha and took 500 monks to Gayāsīsa, the Buddha sent Sāriputta and Moggallāna after them. Devadatta invited Sāriputta to teach while he rested and then fell asleep. Sāriputta and Moggallāna took that moment to teach the monks and lead them back.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha’s two chief disciples, sent as envoys into a hostile assembly, waited for the right time and place before speaking.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s kālam karuti, iṭaṉ aṟintu: choosing the moment and setting before delivering the message.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good narrative match on timing within a mission.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Shipwrecked and naked, Odysseus wonders whether to clasp the princess Nausicaa’s knees or to plead from a distance with gentle words. He decides to stand apart and speak, so as not to anger her.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer shows Odysseus weighing place, manner and words before speaking to someone whose help he needs.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s eṇṇi uraippāṉ: the speaker who thinks through where and how to speak before he opens his mouth.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Vivid match on deliberation; Odysseus is a suppliant, not an envoy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates tells Phaedrus that a true speaker must first learn the different kinds of soul and which kinds of speech persuade each. He must then be able to recognise them quickly in real life, and must add to this a knowledge of the right times for speaking and for keeping silent before his art is complete.
philosophy.explanation: In the closing discussion of rhetoric, Plato makes knowledge of the listener, together with a sense of the right moment (kairos) for each kind of speech, a condition of any real art of persuasion.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato's speaker, like the Kural's ideal envoy, must judge the audience and the moment before choosing his words.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; this section could not be loaded verbatim in this session (the MIT and Perseus pages failed to load or were cut off before 271), so no quotation marks are used. Partial-to-strong match on timing and knowing one's hearer; Plato is describing the orator in general rather than an envoy, and he says nothing about protocol or place.

kurals.tamil:
தூய்மை துணைமை துணிவுடைமை இம்மூன்றின்
வாய்மை வழியுரைப்பான் பண்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Thooymai thunaimai thunivudaimai immoondrin
Vaaymai vazhiyuraippaan panbu.
kurals.meaning: The one who carries his master’s message exactly as given must have purity, supporters, and boldness, and truthfulness together with these three.
kurals.elementary: When your teacher gives you a note for your parents, you shouldn’t swap the words for a treat, you should have a grown-up nearby who can help, you should be brave enough to deliver it even if it’s bad news, and you must never change what it says.
kurals.university: From here Parimelazhagar turns to the second kind of envoy, the vazhi uraippāṉ, who repeats his king’s words exactly as spoken. He gives each quality a job. Tūymai is purity from greed for wealth or women (poruḷ kāmaṅkaḷ), so bribes cannot bend the message. Tuṇaimai is having the foreign ministers’ support, so that if the envoy’s praise of his own king angers them, they can smooth it over by saying ‘that is how our people speak’. Tuṇivuṭaimai is boldness, so he does not hold back out of fear of harm. Vāymai is truthfulness, so everyone can trust him. He reads ‘immūṉṟiṉ’ with the -iṉ in the sense of ‘together with’: truthfulness is a fourth quality alongside the three. Manakkudavar differs: tuṇaimai is having kin, tuṇivu is resolving after inquiry. Pappaiah follows Parimelazhagar closely. On the text: all sources agree; the sandhi-joined text writes யிம்மூன்றின்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Before the war, Dhritarashtra sends his charioteer Sanjaya to the Pandavas. Sanjaya is trusted on both sides for his honesty. He delivers the king’s message and carries Yudhishthira’s reply faithfully back to the Kaurava court.
hinduism.explanation: Sanjaya is a messenger valued above all for integrity and accurate reporting.
hinduism.tie_back: He fits the Kural’s vazhi uraippāṉ, the envoy whose purity and truthfulness make him trusted by both courts.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Sanjaya-yana sections (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: A genuine envoy known for honesty; the ‘supporters’ element is not stressed.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man’s conscience in the sight of God.”
christianity.explanation: Paul insists that he passes on the message entrusted to him without falsifying it, and wins trust through truthfulness.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s tūymai and vāymai: a messenger who does not tamper with what he was given.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on purity and truthful transmission; supporters and boldness are not addressed.

islam.quote_or_event: At al-Hudaybiyya, the Prophet chose ‘Uthman ibn ‘Affan as envoy to the Quraysh partly because his clan in Mecca could protect him. A kinsman there gave him protection while he delivered the message.
islam.explanation: The envoy was picked in part because he had allies in the other camp.
islam.tie_back: This is Parimelazhagar’s tuṇaimai: supporters at the foreign court who keep the envoy safe and the talks smooth.
islam.source: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (trans. A. Guillaume), account of al-Hudaybiyya
islam._accuracy_note: Clear illustration of the ‘supporters’ quality; the other qualities are implied.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A wicked messenger falleth into mischief: but a faithful ambassador is health.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb contrasts the damage a corrupt messenger causes with the good a faithful envoy brings.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural too makes faithfulness and purity the envoy’s defining traits.
judaism._accuracy_note: Explicit ambassador proverb on faithfulness; does not list the Kural’s other qualities.

buddhism.quote_or_event: King Ajātasattu sends his minister Vassakāra to the Buddha with instructions to repeat his question exactly and bring back exactly what the Buddha says, since Tathāgatas do not speak falsely. Vassakāra does both.
buddhism.explanation: The minister acts as a word-for-word envoy between the king and the Buddha.
buddhism.tie_back: He is a clear example of the Kural’s vazhi uraippāṉ, the one who carries a message exactly as given.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Exact type of envoy; the specific virtues are not listed.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Answering the embassy, Achilles says he hates like the gates of Hades the man who hides one thing in his heart and says another, and that he will therefore speak plainly.
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles demands transparent truthfulness in the envoys’ exchange and practises it himself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: His ideal is the Kural’s vāymai, truthfulness joined to boldness.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: The speaker is the recipient of the embassy, not the envoy, but the ideal of candour is exact.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Harold Nicolson named truthfulness the first quality of the ideal diplomat, followed by precision, calm, good temper, patience, modesty and loyalty. He argued that a negotiator’s lasting credit rests on never deceiving.
philosophy.explanation: A twentieth-century diplomat’s classic study puts moral reliability at the centre of the envoy’s craft.
philosophy.tie_back: Nicolson’s truthfulness and loyalty match the Kural’s vāymai and tūymai.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of Nicolson’s well-known list; chapter reference approximate.

kurals.tamil:
விடுமாற்றம் வேந்தர்க்கு உரைப்பான் வடுமாற்றம்
வாய்சேரா வன்க ணவன்.
kurals.transliteration:
Vidumaatram vendharkku uraippaan vadumaatram
Vaaysera vankanavan.
kurals.meaning: Only a man firm enough never to let a shameful word slip out, even under pressure, is fit to carry his king’s message to other kings.
kurals.elementary: Suppose you are sent to tell a bigger kid that your friend wants his bike back. If the big kid scares you, it’s tempting to say ‘my friend is silly, never mind’. A good messenger stays strong and never says something that makes the person who sent him look bad.
kurals.university: Viṭu māṟṟam is ‘the word sent’, the king’s message. Vaṭu māṟṟam is ‘a word that scars’. Parimelazhagar explains this as words that lower one’s own king, which the envoy might say out of fear of harm to himself. Vaṉkaṇ is the firmness never to let such words out, even by a slip of the tongue (vāy cōrntum). He says ‘vaṭu’ (a scar) was chosen because such lowering goes against the duty of one’s station (cāti tarumam). He also notes that ‘vāy cērā’ expresses the result (not speaking) through its cause (firmness). Manakkudavar calls the quality añcāmai, fearlessness. Pappaiah and Kalaignar stress not saying anything wrong or demeaning when danger threatens. On the text: ytamizh.com prints the couplet without a final stop; thirukkural.net and the sandhi-joined text have வன்க ணவன். in the metrical division; thirukkuralvilakkam.blogspot.com joins it as வன்கணவன். Some editions give வாய்சோரா for வாய்சேரா (Parimelazhagar’s gloss uses ‘வாய்சோர்ந்தும்’), but the sources consulted read வாய்சேரா.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya tells the envoy to deliver his king’s message exactly as entrusted, even if weapons are raised against him, and to bear whatever the enemy says without betraying his master. Because envoys are the mouthpieces of kings, they are not to be killed.
hinduism.explanation: The Arthashastra makes faithful, unflinching delivery the envoy’s first duty under threat.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s vaṉkaṇ: the firmness that keeps a message intact and free of any disgrace to the king under pressure.
hinduism._accuracy_note: A close match in the same chapter on envoys; paraphrased.

christianity.quote_or_event: Frightened in the high priest’s courtyard, Peter denies three times that he knows Jesus. When the cock crows he remembers Jesus’ words and weeps bitterly.
christianity.explanation: Under fear, the chief disciple says words that dishonour the master he represents, and he bitterly regrets it.
christianity.tie_back: It is a warning example of the Kural’s vaṭu māṟṟam, the shameful word that slips out when firmness fails.
christianity._accuracy_note: A counter-example that fits the fear-driven slip exactly; Peter is not formally an envoy here.

islam.quote_or_event: “What do you believe yourselves? They said: We believe as he believes. He said: I swear by Allah that were it not that messengers are not killed, I would cut off your heads.”
islam.explanation: Musaylimah’s envoys stand by their master’s claim even in front of the Prophet, and the Prophet spares them because envoys are not to be killed.
islam.tie_back: They do not back away from their sender’s message under pressure. This is the Kural’s firmness, though the cause they served was rejected.
islam._accuracy_note: Shows envoys holding firm and envoy immunity; the moral standing of their message is the opposite of praiseworthy.

judaism.quote_or_event: Avtalyon warns scholars to be careful with their words. A careless phrase could lead students into error, and in the end the name of Heaven would be profaned.
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah teaches that a representative’s careless words bring disgrace on the one he represents.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s envoy must likewise never let slip a word that stains the name of the king who sent him.
judaism._accuracy_note: Right principle of guarding speech for the sender’s honour; set in teaching, not diplomacy.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells Prince Abhaya that he never speaks words that are untrue or unbeneficial. Even true and beneficial words he speaks only when he knows the time is right, whether or not they are welcome.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha keeps strict control over what leaves his mouth, weighing truth, benefit and timing.
buddhism.tie_back: This kind of self-mastery in speech is what keeps the Kural’s envoy from letting a harmful word slip.
buddhism._accuracy_note: General discipline of speech; the envoy setting and fear are not present.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Trojan herald Idaeus brings Paris’s offer to the Greek camp. While delivering it, he adds his own wish that Paris had died before causing all this.
greek_mythology.explanation: Idaeus lets words slip that shame the side he represents while he is delivering their official message.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He is the envoy the Kural rules out: one who lets a vaṭu māṟṟam, a disgraceful word, pass his lips.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A counter-example from a real embassy; exact line numbers approximate.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But I thought that I ought not to do anything common or mean in the hour of danger: nor do I now repent of the manner of my defence, and I would rather die having spoken after my manner, than speak in your manner and live.”
philosophy.explanation: After being condemned, Socrates explains why he would not weep, plead or bring his children into court to win pity, saying that he would rather die than save himself with words unworthy of him.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural's envoy, Socrates holds that no pressure, even the threat of death, should force a shameful word from a man of firm character.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Jowett). Partial match: the shared point is firmness against saying anything base under threat. Socrates is defending himself, however, not carrying a king's message to other kings.

kurals.tamil:
இறுதி பயப்பினும் எஞ்சாது இறைவற்கு
உறுதி பயப்பதாம் தூது.
kurals.transliteration:
Irudhi payappinum enjaadhu iraivarku
Urudhi payappadhaam thoodhu.
kurals.meaning: The true envoy delivers his king’s message in full and secures his king’s good, holding nothing back, even if it costs him his life.
kurals.elementary: Think of a lifeguard who swims out to someone in trouble even though the waves are scary. A true messenger is like that. Even when delivering the message is frightening or dangerous, they carry it all the way for the people who trusted them.
kurals.university: Iṟuti is ‘end’, meaning death. Eñcātu is ‘without leaving any of it out’. Uṟuti is ‘firm good’ or advantage. Parimelazhagar: even if the words will end the envoy’s life, he does not hold back out of fear, and he speaks his king’s position to foreign kings exactly as told. He adds that by naming death, the worst outcome, Valluvar leaves lesser dangers without need of mention. With 688-690 the chapter completes its account of the envoy who repeats a given message (kūṟiyatu kūṟuvāṉ). The couplet ends the chapter on its highest demand, loyalty to the death, and prepares for chapter 70 on conduct in the king’s presence. All modern commentators (Varadarasanar, Pappaiah, Kalaignar) read iṟuti as the envoy’s own death. On the text: the sandhi-joined text reads பயப்பினு மெஞ்சா திறைவற் / குறுதி, the same wording as the split form.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Sent by Rama to Ravana with a final ultimatum, Angada delivers it in full in the demon king’s own court. When Ravana orders him seized, Angada leaps onto the palace roof carrying his captors and breaks its peak before returning.
hinduism.explanation: Angada carries his master’s ultimatum into the enemy’s hall and gives all of it, knowing he may be killed.
hinduism.tie_back: He fits the Kural’s envoy who holds nothing back even when the embassy may cost his life.
hinduism._accuracy_note: A genuine envoy under mortal threat delivering the whole message.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But none of these things move me, neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus, to testify the gospel of the grace of God.”
christianity.explanation: Warned that chains await him, Paul says his life matters less than finishing the commission he was given.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s iṟuti payappiṉum eñcātu: carrying out the commission even at the cost of one’s life.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close match on putting the mission ahead of life.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet’s envoy al-Harith ibn ‘Umayr al-Azdi, carrying a letter to the ruler of Busra, was seized and killed by the Ghassanid chief Shurahbil ibn ‘Amr. The killing of this envoy led to the expedition of Mu’ta.
islam.explanation: The sira remembers an envoy who died carrying his master’s letter, and treats killing him as a grave violation.
islam.tie_back: It makes real the Kural’s case in which the embassy ‘yields death’ (iṟuti payappiṉum).
islam.source: al-Waqidi, Kitab al-Maghazi; Ibn Sa‘d, Tabaqat (account of Mu’ta)
islam._accuracy_note: Reported in the maghazi literature; details of the envoy’s own conduct are sparse.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Go, gather together all the Jews that are present in Shushan, and fast ye for me … and so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish.”
judaism.explanation: Esther goes before the Persian king uninvited to plead for her people, knowing it could mean death.
judaism.tie_back: ‘If I perish, I perish’ is the spirit of the Kural’s envoy, who does not hold back though death may follow.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match on risking death to carry a plea to a king; Esther is an intercessor, not a formal envoy.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Before going to teach among the fierce people of Sunāparanta, the monk Puṇṇa tells the Buddha how he will meet each threat, including being killed, without resentment. The Buddha then sends him, and he wins many followers there.
buddhism.explanation: Puṇṇa accepts that his mission may end in his death and goes anyway.
buddhism.tie_back: He shows the Kural’s envoy who does not turn back even when the mission may end his life.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match on accepting death for a mission; he is sent by a teacher, not a king.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After Sparta killed Persian heralds, two Spartan nobles, Sperthias and Boulis, volunteered to go to Xerxes and give their lives in atonement. Xerxes refused to kill them.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek tradition held heralds sacred under Hermes, and these envoys went knowingly to their deaths for their city.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s envoy, they carried out their mission for their state knowing it would probably kill them.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Historical tradition rather than myth, used because no closer mythic parallel exists.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero tells how Marcus Atilius Regulus, a captive of Carthage, was sent to Rome on oath to negotiate a prisoner exchange. He advised the Senate against it because it harmed Rome, then kept his oath and went back to Carthage to be tortured to death.
philosophy.explanation: Cicero holds Regulus up as the model of an envoy who puts his country’s good and his given word above his life.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s envoy almost exactly: he secures his country’s good (uṟuti) though his own death (iṟuti) follows.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near-perfect match: an envoy who chose his country’s advantage over his own life.
